newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg suburb flooded but city's defense holds.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg suburb flooded but city's defense holds.

text.p: The swollen Red River flooded a village on the outskirts of Winnipeg on Saturday, destroying about 100 homes, but the water failed to breach the defenses protecting the heart of Manitoba's biggest city.
The upscale community of Grande Pointe, home to about 325 people on the southeast edge of Winnipeg, was the latest victim of the surging "Red Sea" that devastated North Dakota and southern Manitoba.
"We spent the night shoring up the north dike. Six of us worked for the last 24 hours. We don't have enough sandbags," said exhausted Grande Pointe resident Claude Lemoine.

Despite the waters lapping at its flanks, Winnipeg, a city of 650,000, kept flooding at bay through a frantic campaign to strengthen dikes, erect sandbag barriers and pump water from areas where the defenses were leaking.

One trouble spot was a leaking dike near a sewage treatment plant on the city's south side. A city spokesman said on Saturday workers were trying to save the dike but that Canadian army engineers had given up hope. If it bursts, residents of the Fort Richmond neighborhood will be forced to evacuate.

The city's savior has been a massive 29-mile (47-km) ditch known as the Floodway that splits the Red River as it enters Winnipeg. It diverts the waters around the city and was built after a devastating 1950 flood forced 100,000 residents from their homes.
The city will not be able to claim victory until Tuesday or Wednesday when the water is forecast to begin dropping. But after weeks of anxiety, officials were optimistic.
"It's obviously a much more positive day," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said late Friday. "It's too early to say we've won because the crest will be in our city for four or five days."
"If the weather changes, we're right back into very high anxiety," Thompson added.
The Red River crested at 24.5 feet (7.5 metres) above winter ice level at downtown Winnipeg at 11 p.m. EDT on Thursday and should hold at that level for about five days.

The flooding -- the worst in the region since 1852 -- forced about 29,000 Canadian and 50,000 Americans to flee their homes. Four Canadians died and property damage was estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars in Canada and $1 billion in North Dakota.
The Red River swelled to 22 times its normal flow last month as record-breaking winter snow melted, flooding an area in southern Manitoba twice the size of Hong Kong.

In Grande Pointe, about 50 of the village's approximately 325 residents worked through Friday night in a desperate bid to save the town. They ferried sandbags in a flotilla of small boats to shore up dikes. Most residents abandoned their homes Thursday when the government issued an evacuation order.
By Saturday morning officials reported that 100 of the area's 150 homes -- many new and expensive -- were lost.

Local residents accused government officials of callously allowing floodwater to inundate the community. The province on Friday diverted more water through the Floodway, raising the water level south of the city. Grande Pointe is just 100 yards (metres) away from the Floodway.
"There's no doubt in my mind we're being sacrificed," said Lemoine.
The government countered that it had no choice but to divert more water through the Floodway or risk jeopardizing many homes inside Winnipeg itself.
